fixes.explanation: That's it, baker. God says, “…the land itself must observe a Sabbath to the LORD.” Not just the people. Verse 4 says the seventh year is “…a Sabbath of complete rest for the land…” and that's a whole year off. I know folks who can't rest half as well as a field can.

A resting shovel sounds lovely, and I bet my stamper handle would sign up fast. But God doesn't name the tools. He says, “…the land itself must observe a Sabbath to the LORD.” What He rules out in that seventh year is sowing the field and pruning the vineyard (Leviticus 25:4).

Yes, baker. God says to sound the horn “…on the tenth day of the seventh month, the Day of Atonement.” He says to sound it throughout the land. That's a big day on the calendar, and the horn is meant to go far and wide.

The Feast of Tabernacles is a fun one, and I see why it popped into your head. But this verse names a different day. The horn is sounded on the tenth day of the seventh month, the Day of Atonement. God says to sound it throughout the land.

Gleaning is a fair guess, baker, but it isn't what God says for liberty. The instruction is that each of you is to return to his property and to his clan. About the fields in that year, God says, “…you are not to sow the land or reap its aftergrowth or harvest the untended vines.” So the fields rest while the people head home.

Yes. More years before the Jubilee means more harvests to sell, so God says you “…shall increase the price in proportion to a greater number of years…” The buyer gets more harvests, so he pays more. It's like a big batch of cookies costing more than a half dozen.

Right. Fewer years left means fewer harvests, so God says to “…decrease it in proportion to a lesser number of years…” Then He gives the reason: “for he is selling you a given number of harvests.” So the buyer pays for the harvests that are left.

Hidden doesn't fit, baker. Both sides count the years since the last Jubilee and the harvest years remaining, and the price follows that count. God also says, “Do not take advantage of each other…” (Leviticus 25:17). A price set by a count of years is the opposite of a mystery.

That's it. God says to keep His statutes and carefully observe His judgments “…so that you may dwell securely in the land.” Verse 19 adds that they can eat their fill and dwell in safety. Security and a full belly, that's what He says follows.
No king is mentioned in this passage. God says the land can't be sold permanently “…because it is Mine…” The deed is His. And He calls the Israelites “…foreigners and residents with Me.”

Right. God says, “…his nearest of kin may come and redeem what his brother has sold.” Notice the word may, so the door is open for a close relative to step in. Having someone like that around is a gift.

The high priest isn't named in these verses. God says it's the man's nearest of kin who may come and redeem what his brother sold. And if the man prospers and acquires enough, he can redeem the land himself (Leviticus 25:26-27). The high priest never enters this picture.
The elders are a fair guess, baker, but they aren't mentioned here. The verse says his nearest of kin may come and redeem what was sold. No city meeting needed, just a close relative stepping up.

Yes. God says, “…he shall calculate the years since its sale, repay the balance to the man to whom he sold it, and return to his property.” It's a count of years, and then home he goes. Years are what this whole chapter counts, from the Sabbath year to the Jubilee.

Tithes are a good guess, but they don't come up in this part of the chapter. The man calculates the years since the sale and repays the balance to the buyer. Then he returns to his property. This math runs on years, friend.

That's right. If he can't get enough to repay, the land stays with the buyer only until the Year of Jubilee. Then God says, “In the Jubilee, however, it is to be released, so that he may return to his property.” So the sale has an end date built in.

Yes. God says to help him “…as you would a foreigner or stranger, so that he can continue to live among you.” The goal is for him to stay in the community. So the help is aimed at keeping him in the neighborhood.

Leaving it to his clan is a fair guess, baker, but it isn't what God says. He tells the people, “…you are to help him as you would a foreigner or stranger, so that he can continue to live among you.” The word is help, and the people hearing it are the ones He's talking to. Nobody gets to wave this one off and hope for the best.

A tenth of his harvest is a fair guess, but the passage never brings it up here. God says, “Do not take any interest or profit from him, but fear your God, that your countryman may live among you.” That's the thing He rules out. The point is that a man in need can keep living among them.

Yes. God says, “…you must not force him into slave labor.” Instead he stays “…as a hired worker or temporary resident…” and works for the buyer until the Year of Jubilee. That's a hired worker's arrangement, not a slave's.

A prisoner isn't in the picture, baker. God says the man stays as a hired worker or temporary resident, and he works until the Year of Jubilee. Nothing in these verses calls him a prisoner. It describes a worker with an end date.

Yes! God says, “Then he and his children are to be released, and he may return to his clan and to the property of his fathers.” The Year of Jubilee frees the man and his children. And the way back to his clan and his fathers' property is open to him.

It's true, baker. In the Year of Jubilee, “…he and his children are to be released, and he may return to his clan and to the property of his fathers.” (Leviticus 25:41) The Jubilee frees him and his children. And the way home to his clan is open.

That's right. God says, “Because the Israelites are My servants, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt, they are not to be sold as slaves.” Their belonging starts with Him. Verse 55 says it again: “For the Israelites are My servants.”

A vow at Sinai is a fair guess, since Moses is on Mount Sinai when this chapter opens (Leviticus 25:1). But no vow is named in these verses. God gives His own reason: He brought them out of the land of Egypt, and they are His servants. That's why none of them is to be sold as slaves.

That's right. God says, “…as for your brothers, the Israelites, no man may rule harshly over his brother.” (Leviticus 25:46) He says the same in verse 43: “You are not to rule over them harshly, but you shall fear your God.” So under these rules, harshness toward a fellow Israelite is ruled out in both places.

Yes. The word in the text is redeem, and here it means someone pays the price to buy him back. God says one of his brothers may redeem him, and then lists his uncle, his cousin or any close relative from his clan. If he prospers, he may even redeem himself.

Not quite, baker. God says, “Even if he is not redeemed in any of these ways, he and his children shall be released in the Year of Jubilee.” (Leviticus 25:54) So the Jubilee frees him either way. Being bought back isn't the only road out.

Right. Even if nobody buys him back, God says, “…he and his children shall be released in the Year of Jubilee.” (Leviticus 25:54) The Jubilee frees him, and his children go free with him. Redemption is one way out, and the Jubilee is there even without it.
